data.title: Can Elicio Therapeutics (NASDAQ:ELTX) Afford To Invest In Growth?
data.description:
Even when a business is losing money, it's possible for shareholders to make money if they buy a good business at the right price. For example, although software-as-a-service business Salesforce.com lost money for years while it grew recurring revenue, if you held shares since 2005, you'd have done very well indeed. Having said that, unprofitable companies are risky because they could potentially burn through all their cash and become distressed.

Given this risk, we thought we'd take a look at whether Elicio Therapeutics (NASDAQ:ELTX) shareholders should be worried about its cash burn. In this report, we will consider the company's annual negative free cash flow, henceforth referring to it as the 'cash burn'. The first step is to compare its cash burn with its cash reserves, to give us its 'cash runway'.

How Long Is Elicio Therapeutics' Cash Runway?

You can calculate a company's cash runway by dividing the amount of cash it has by the rate at which it is spending that cash. When Elicio Therapeutics last reported its September 2026 balance sheet in November 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth US$31m. Looking at the last year, the company burnt through US$38m. Therefore, from September 2026 it had roughly 10 months of cash runway. That's quite a short cash runway, indicating the company must either reduce its annual cash burn or replenish its cash. You can see how its cash balance has changed over time in the image below.

How Is Elicio Therapeutics' Cash Burn Changing Over Time?

Because Elicio Therapeutics isn't currently generating revenue, we consider it an early-stage business. So while we can't look to sales to understand growth, we can look at how the cash burn is changing to understand how expenditure is trending over time. It's possible that the 3.2% reduction in cash burn over the last year is evidence of management tightening their belts as cash reserves deplete. Clearly, however, the crucial factor is whether the company will grow its business going forward. So you might want to take a peek at how much the company is expected to grow in the next few years.

How Easily Can Elicio Therapeutics Raise Cash?

Even though it has reduced its cash burn recently, shareholders should still consider how easy it would be for Elicio Therapeutics to raise more cash in the future. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. One of the main advantages held by publicly listed companies is that they can sell shares to investors to raise cash and fund growth. By looking at a company's cash burn relative to its market capitalisation, we gain insight on how much shareholders would be diluted if the company needed to raise enough cash to cover another year's cash burn.

In the last year, Elicio Therapeutics burned through US$38m, which is just about equal to its US$37m market cap. Given just how high that expenditure is, relative to the company's market value, we think there's an elevated risk of funding distress, and we would be very nervous about holding the stock.

So, Should We Worry About Elicio Therapeutics' Cash Burn?

Even though its cash burn relative to its market cap makes us a little nervous, we are compelled to mention that we thought Elicio Therapeutics' cash burn reduction was relatively promising. data.title: Just Four Days Till Diamondback Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:FANG) Will Be Trading Ex-Dividend
data.description:
Readers hoping to buy Diamondback Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:FANG) for its dividend will need to make their move shortly, as the stock is about to trade ex-dividend. The ex-dividend date is usually set to be one business day before the record date, which is the cut-off date on which you must be present on the company's books as a shareholder in order to receive the dividend. The ex-dividend date is an important date to be aware of as any purchase of the stock made on or after this date might mean a late settlement that doesn't show on the record date. Meaning, you will need to purchase Diamondback Energy's shares before the 12th of November to receive the dividend, which will be paid on the 19th of November.

The company's next dividend payment will be US$1.18 per share, on the back of last year when the company paid a total of US$4.72 to shareholders. Calculating the last year's worth of payments shows that Diamondback Energy has a trailing yield of 2.6% on the current share price of US$178.96. Dividends are an important source of income to many shareholders, but the health of the business is crucial to maintaining those dividends. So we need to check whether the dividend payments are covered, and if earnings are growing.

If a company pays out more in dividends than it earned, then the dividend might become unsustainable - hardly an ideal situation. Diamondback Energy is paying out an acceptable 61% of its profit, a common payout level among most companies. Yet cash flow is typically more important than profit for assessing dividend sustainability, so we should always check if the company generated enough cash to afford its dividend. It distributed 28% of its free cash flow as dividends, a comfortable payout level for most companies.

It's positive to see that Diamondback Energy's dividend is covered by both profits and cash flow, since this is generally a sign that the dividend is sustainable, and a lower payout ratio usually suggests a greater margin of safety before the dividend gets cut.

Have Earnings And Dividends Been Growing?

Companies with falling earnings are riskier for dividend shareholders. If earnings fall far enough, the company could be forced to cut its dividend. Readers will understand then, why we're concerned to see Diamondback Energy's earnings per share have dropped 14% a year over the past five years. Ultimately, when earnings per share decline, the size of the pie from which dividends can be paid, shrinks.

Another key way to measure a company's dividend prospects is by measuring its historical rate of dividend growth. Diamondback Energy has delivered 28% dividend growth per year on average over the past nine years. Growing the dividend payout ratio while earnings are declining can deliver nice returns for a while, but it's always worth checking for when the company can't increase the payout ratio any more - because then the music stops.

The Bottom Line

From a dividend perspective, should investors buy or avoid Diamondback Energy? We're not enthused by the declining earnings per share, although at least the company's payout ratio is within a reasonable range, meaning it may not be at imminent risk of a dividend cut. The fresh earnings beat and dividend lift have coincided with a sharp pick up in momentum, with Sprott’s share price up 2.19% on the day and 13.72% over the past week, while the 1 year total shareholder return of 29.06% and the very large 3 year total shareholder return near 4x indicate that long term holders have already experienced strong compounding.

Sprott’s latest jump and long run of strong total returns raise a simple question: Is the real opportunity still ahead at CA$161.11, or has most of the upside already played out on this move?

Price-to-Earnings of 25.7x: Is it justified?

Sprott now trades on a P/E of 25.7x, which puts the CA$161.11 share price on a much richer footing than both its industry and peer averages.

The P/E ratio compares what investors pay for each dollar of current earnings. For an asset manager like Sprott, that figure often reflects how confident the market feels about the durability and quality of those profits.

High quality earnings, a 27.2% return on equity and profit growth of 29.2% per year over five years indicate that investors are paying up for a business that has converted past performance into stronger profitability. That sort of earnings profile can justify a premium P/E when investors are comfortable that margins and returns on equity can be supported.

The gap to the broader Canadian Capital Markets group is wide. Sprott trades at 25.7x earnings, while the industry average is 7.9x and the peer group average is 8.1x, which signals that the market is assigning a much higher valuation to its profit stream than it does to comparable firms.

Result: Price-to-Earnings of 25.7x (OVERVALUED)

Still, the recent 1 year and 3 year total shareholder returns, together with a richer 25.7x P/E, could leave Sprott exposed if revenue pressure persists or sentiment toward critical materials cools.

Another View: Our DCF model points the other way

The P/E story paints Sprott as expensive, yet our DCF model says something very different. At CA$161.11, the share price sits well above an estimated future cash flow value of CA$52.11. This frames the stock as heavily overvalued on this second lens.

This kind of gap can matter in practical terms. If cash flows do not stretch to meet that richer market price, investors are relying on sentiment and optimism to keep the multiple where it is or push it higher. That sets up a simple question for anyone looking at Sprott today: Which signal feels more reliable, the premium P/E or the discounted cash flow math?

data.title: Gold.com, Inc. Just Missed Earnings - But Analysts Have Updated Their Models
data.description:
The analysts might have been a bit too bullish on Gold.com, Inc. (NYSE:GOLD), given that the company fell short of expectations when it released its first-quarter results last week. Gold.com delivered a grave earnings miss, with both revenues (US$3.3b) and statutory earnings per share (US$0.05) falling badly short of analyst expectations. Earnings are an important time for investors, as they can track a company's performance, look at what the analysts are forecasting for next year, and see if there's been a change in sentiment towards the company. So we gathered the latest post-earnings forecasts to see what estimates suggest is in store for next year.

Trump has pledged to "unleash" American oil and gas and these 15 US stocks have developments that are poised to benefit.

Following the recent earnings report, the consensus from four analysts covering Gold.com is for revenues of US$21.5b in 2027. This implies a not inconsiderable 14% decline in revenue compared to the last 12 months. Statutory per-share earnings are expected to be US$2.90, roughly flat on the last 12 months. Before this earnings report, the analysts had been forecasting revenues of US$21.5b and earnings per share (EPS) of US$2.74 in 2027. So the consensus seems to have become somewhat more optimistic on Gold.com's earnings potential following these results.

See our latest analysis for Gold.com

The consensus price target was unchanged at US$64.40, implying that the improved earnings outlook is not expected to have a long term impact on value creation for shareholders. It could also be instructive to look at the range of analyst estimates, to evaluate how different the outlier opinions are from the mean. The most optimistic Gold.com analyst has a price target of US$90.00 per share, while the most pessimistic values it at US$52.00. As you can see, analysts are not all in agreement on the stock's future, but the range of estimates is still reasonably narrow, which could suggest that the outcome is not totally unpredictable.

These estimates are interesting, but it can be useful to paint some more broad strokes when seeing how forecasts compare, both to the Gold.com's past performance and to peers in the same industry. These estimates imply that revenue is expected to slow, with a forecast annualised decline of 19% by the end of 2027. This indicates a significant reduction from annual growth of 24% over the last five years. By contrast, our data suggests that other companies (with analyst coverage) in the same industry are forecast to see their revenue grow 3.2% annually for the foreseeable future. It's pretty clear that Gold.com's revenues are expected to perform substantially worse than the wider industry.

The Bottom Line

The biggest takeaway for us is the consensus earnings per share upgrade, which suggests a clear improvement in sentiment around Gold.com's earnings potential next year. On the plus side, there were no major changes to revenue estimates; although forecasts imply they will perform worse than the wider industry. The consensus price target held steady at US$64.40, with the latest estimates not enough to have an impact on their price targets.

Following on from that line of thought, we think that the long-term prospects of the business are much more relevant than next year's earnings. We have forecasts for Gold.com going out to 2029, and you can see them free on our platform here.
